subject: 💰 A different IPO boom

Plus: Distress call | Wednesday, October 14, 2026

Axios Closer
By Nathan Bomey · Oct 14, 2026

Wednesday ✅.

Today's newsletter is 826 words, a 3-minute read.

📉 The dashboard: The S&P 500 closed down 1.1%.

  • Inflation gained steam in September, with the annual CPI rate hitting 3.7%, fueling bets on an interest rate hike later this month.
  • AI stocks fell on renewed concerns over debt financing the industry's massive buildout. (See below.👇)

🔥 Today's stock spotlight: Bending Spoons (+41.2%), the tech conglomerate, soared following the disclosure of a new $330 million investment from Berkshire Hathaway.
 
 
1 big thing: A different IPO boom
 

Illustration: Gabriella Turrisi/Axios
 

The IPO boom is turning into a windfall for Morgan Stanley's wealth management business as newly public companies create a fresh wave of rich clients.

Why it matters: While Wall Street banks make money from underwriting IPOs, they can also score big by managing the newfound wealth of founders, executives and employees after their companies go public.

💸 Driving the news: Morgan Stanley's wealth management unit took in more than $116 billion in new client assets connected to IPOs in its latest quarter, the company reported today.

  • Overall, the unit reported $232 billion in net new assets, which was about $150 billion+ more than the same period a year earlier.
  • Wealth management revenue rose 10.1% to a record $9.1 billion, including a 15.8% increase in asset management revenue to $5.5 billion.

🔍 Between the lines: Morgan Stanley has spent years building a pipeline of potential wealth management clients by managing employee stock compensation plans for private companies.

  • When those companies go public, the bank is well-positioned to turn their employees into wealth customers.
  • In July, CFO Sharon Yeshaya told investors that Morgan Stanley had "about 70% of the top 100 unicorns" in its workplace pipeline.
  • "We've spent a lot of time thinking about how do we service some of these companies at the very early stages," she said.

"With an active IPO calendar, the pace of our funnel accelerates and client interest in advice increases," Yeshaya said on today's call.

  • "While flows will fluctuate as lockups expire, funds make distributions and individuals use assets for consumption, our pipeline and our connectivity across channels allow us to build relationships early and deepen them over time."

By the numbers: U.S. IPO proceeds topped $141 billion through early July, according to data from Renaissance Capital, Axios Pro's Lucinda Shen reported.

  • That put it on the precipice of topping 2021's record $142.4 billion mark, powered in part by the all-time U.S. record with SpaceX.

What we're watching: The widely expected IPOs of Anthropic and OpenAI — and which investment banks get their business.

The bottom line: For Wall Street, the IPO payday can begin long before a company goes public — and continue long after the shares start trading.
 
 
2. Netflix cuts 1,000 employees
 

Photo: Michael Yanow/NurPhoto via Getty Images
 

Netflix plans to lay off 6% of its global workforce, or roughly 1,000 employees, in an effort to better position itself for future investments, its co-CEOs told employees today, Axios' Sara Fischer reports.

Why it matters: Co-CEO Ted Sarandos acknowledged last month in a Bloomberg interview that the company is not growing as fast as he would like.

🔍 Zoom in: The cuts are expected to mostly impact the company's business functions, including human resources, product, technology and legal teams, per a source familiar with the situation.

  • The company said it still expects to meet investor expectations for its full-year financials.

The big picture: Netflix is still the most profitable streaming business among its competitive set, but its focus on streaming means its business isn't as diversified as other entertainment giants, who can offset a competitive streaming market with things like theme parks and products.
 
 
3. Other happenings
 

Illustration: Allie Carl/Axios
 

📉 Gartner analysts estimated that more than $3.5 billion in AI infrastructure spending "could be exposed to impairment by the end of 2030, if AI providers continue their current pace of capital" investment. (Gartner)

🤖 OpenAI CFO Sara Friar warned that low-cost Chinese AI models expose users to cybersecurity risks. Chinese open-weight models present a competitive threat to OpenAI's closed models. (Bloomberg)

🏦 Bank of America shares tumbled after federal regulators announced a $1.2 billion penalty for the company and then it posted a decline in fixed-income trading revenue. (CNBC)

🇨🇳 Apple is preparing to release its AI platform in mainland China in December, following years of regulatory delay. (Bloomberg)

4. 🗣️ Quoted: Distress call
 

Photo: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images
 
"Yikes."
— Elon Musk, on X, responding to a chart posted by Chamath Palihapitiya showing CoreWeave bond yields hitting 15% today. The AI neocloud company's debt is trading at levels that analysts consider distressed, but CEO Mike Intrator told employees that the market is acting "irrationally."

📉 CoreWeave shares closed down 15.5%.
